Received 26 August 2024 l Revised 28 December 2024 l Accepted 4 January 2025 l Published online 30 April 2025 Abstract: Objective: This study aimed to analyze the impact of community mobility on the Corona virus disease 2019 (COVID-19) cases in ASEAN countries using panel data regression. Material and Methods: The Google Mobility Report and World Health Organization (WHO) COVID-19 Global Data were analyzed from February 15, 2020, to October 13, 2022. Three distinct periods were examined: pre-vaccination, vaccination rollout, and post-herd immunity. Panel data regression models were employed to assess the impact of various mobility factors on daily COVID-19 cases. Results: The analysis revealed that mobility patterns significantly influenced COVID-19 case numbers during the pre- vaccination period. As vaccination programs progressed and herd immunity was achieved, the impact of mobility on new cases diminished. The models explained with R2 were between 20.15% and 33.33% of the variations in case numbers across the periods. Conclusion: This study emphasizes the importance of community mobility in COVID-19 transmissions. Effective vaccination strategies and public health measures are crucial in mitigating the impact of mobility on disease spread. JSON: Name: asean_mobility_panel_regression Title: Panel data regression analysis of community mobility effects on daily COVID-19 cases in ASEAN across pre-vaccination, vaccination rollout, and post-herd-immunity periods Short Hypothesis: Increased community mobility (measured by Google mobility indices) causes higher daily confirmed COVID-19 cases in ASEAN countries, and the magnitude of this causal effect decreases as national vaccination coverage increases. Related Work: Prior work has estimated mobility–infection links using cross-sectional, time-series, and panel approaches. Cross-sectional studies identify correlations between mobility indicators and case counts but cannot separate temporal dynamics or unobserved heterogeneity. Time-series analyses capture dynamics within single locations but struggle to generalize across jurisdictions and to control for cross-sectional confounders. Existing panel studies improve control for unobserved country effects but often use short time windows, omit vaccination coverage or variant prevalence as moderators, and do not systematically compare fixed, random, and dynamic panel estimators. Common weaknesses include: potential endogeneity of mobility (behavioral response to case incidence), multicollinearity among mobility categories, inconsistent lag selection for incubation and reporting delays, reliance on imperfect mobility proxies (smartphone users only), limited robustness checks across model specifications, and inadequate handling of heteroskedasticity and serial correlation. No prior work jointly quantifies category-specific mobility effects across distinct vaccination phases in ASEAN while reporting model-selection diagnostics and multiple robustness analyses. Abstract: This study quantifies the causal effect of community mobility on daily confirmed COVID-19 cases in ASEAN using panel data regression across three epidemiological periods: pre-vaccination, vaccination rollout, and post-herd-immunity. Using aggregated Google mobility indices and WHO daily case counts for eight ASEAN countries from February 15, 2020 to October 13, 2022, we estimate pooled, fixed-effects, random-effects, and dynamic panel models with country and time dimensions and a 5-day case lag. The main contribution is a systematic comparison of model families, formal model selection and diagnostic testing, and estimation of how vaccination coverage moderates mobility effects. We report category-specific mobility coefficients, model fit, and out-of-sample forecast performance, and conduct ablations for lag choice, multicollinearity treatment, and inclusion of vaccination–mobility interactions. Expected outcomes include identification of mobility categories that significantly increased transmission in the pre-vaccination period and evidence of attenuated mobility effects as vaccination coverage rose, providing policy-relevant quantification of mobility risks across vaccination phases. Experiments: Datasets: Google COVID-19 Community Mobility Reports (retail & recreation, grocery & pharmacy, parks, transit stations, workplaces, residential) and WHO daily confirmed COVID-19 cases; auxiliary controls: Our World in Data vaccination coverage (fully vaccinated per 100), Oxford Stringency Index, daily tests per 100k, population density, median age, and reported variant prevalence where available. Sample: eight ASEAN countries (Brunei and Vietnam excluded for missing/incomplete mobility data) from 2020-02-15 to 2022-10-13. Preprocess: align by date, compute 5-day lead of cases (cases_t+5) as primary dependent variable; create alternative lead sets (3-, 7-, 14-day) for sensitivity; standardize mobility indices and vaccination rate. Baselines: pooled OLS (common effects), fixed effects (country and time), random effects, two-way random effects, dynamic panel (Arellano-Bond GMM) to include lagged dependent variable, and instrumental-variable (IV) panel with exogenous instruments for mobility (weather variables and public transit strikes/events where available). Model specifications: (a) main: cases_t+5 ~ mobility_categories + vaccination_rate + mobility_categories*vaccination_rate + controls + country FE + time FE; (b) ablation: remove interaction terms; (c) PCA variant: replace mobility categories with first two principal components; (d) lag-sensitivity: run with 3/7/14-day leads; (e) dynamic: include lagged dependent variable and estimate with system GMM. Model selection and diagnostics: run Chow, Hausman, Breusch-Pagan LM; compute VIF for multicollinearity; test heteroskedasticity and serial correlation; report clustered robust standard errors by country and Newey-West where appropriate. Evaluation metrics: in-sample adjusted R^2, AIC/BIC, coefficient point estimates and 95% CI, p-values; out-of-sample rolling-origin forecast RMSE and MAPE with country-wise holdout folds; causal diagnostics: IV relevance (F-statistic), overidentification (Hansen J), and Arellano-Bond autocorrelation tests. Comparison/ablation studies: (1) fixed-effects vs random-effects vs pooled OLS vs system GMM; (2) full model vs no-interaction ablation to quantify moderation by vaccination; (3) mobility-categories model vs PCA-reduced model; (4) alternative lag experiments (3/5/7/14 days) assessing coefficient stability. Statistical thresholds: two-sided tests with alpha=0.05. Power/sample: report degrees of freedom and effect-size detectable with given N×T per period (~392 observations per period as reported). Software: R (plm, lme4, plmtest) and Stata/ivreg2 or equivalent. Risk Factors and Limitations: Data representativeness: Google mobility reflects smartphone users with location history enabled and may bias toward urban, higher-income, or younger populations. Case under-reporting and variable testing rates across countries introduce measurement error and biased dependent variable. Endogeneity: mobility may be endogenous (responds to current/expected case trends) causing biased coefficient estimates if not instrumented or modeled dynamically. Multicollinearity: high correlation among mobility categories can inflate variance of estimates and obscure category-level effects. Lag misspecification: incorrect choice of incubation/reporting lag produces biased effect sizes. Unobserved confounders: variant prevalence, healthcare capacity, and undocumented NPIs can confound estimated mobility effects. Generalizability: findings limited to eight ASEAN countries and the specified time window; exclusion of Brunei and Vietnam reduces representativeness. Model limitations: fixed-effects models cannot estimate time-invariant covariates; dynamic GMM may suffer weak instruments or bias with few time periods. Statistical issues: heteroskedasticity and serial correlation risk invalid inference if not properly addressed; small number of cross-sections limits asymptotic properties of some panel estimators. Computational: system GMM and IV diagnostics require careful tuning and may be unstable with high multicollinearity or weak instruments.
